comments.title: Comment Submitted by Udaya Kumar Velayudam
comments.commentText:
I appreciate the efforts of President Donald Trump and his administration to strengthen the integrity of the U.S. immigration system, address visa misuse, and move toward a merit-based immigration framework. I understand and support the objective of ensuring that employment-based visa holders comply with the requirements of their immigration status.

However, I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposal to eliminate the existing discretionary 60-day grace period for individuals who lose their employment.

Many employment-based visa holders have lived in the United States for several years, contributing to American businesses, paying taxes, raising families, and becoming part of their local communities. Losing a job unexpectedly is already a difficult experience. Requiring individuals and their families to leave the country immediately creates significant practical and financial hardships.

There are several important considerations:

1. Children’s education and family commitments

Many families have children enrolled in American schools. An unexpected job loss should not force parents to abruptly disrupt their children’s education in the middle of an academic semester. Families need reasonable time to arrange school transitions and prepare their children for an international relocation.

2. Financial and contractual obligations

Families have significant financial commitments, including rental agreements, mortgage payments, vehicle loans, insurance, and other contractual obligations. These commitments cannot be terminated overnight without potentially significant financial consequences. A reasonable grace period allows families to settle these responsibilities and avoid unnecessary losses.

3. Practical challenges of international relocation

Relocating an entire family to another country is not as simple as purchasing an airline ticket. Families need time to arrange travel, sell or ship household belongings, close accounts, manage property, coordinate dependent family members, and make arrangements for their children’s education and future.

I fully understand that individuals who no longer qualify for their employment-based visa must eventually depart the United States or obtain another lawful immigration status. I am not suggesting that anyone should be allowed to remain indefinitely after losing qualifying employment.

My concern is that eliminating the 60-day grace period removes the reasonable transition time needed to manage these responsibilities. It could unintentionally put otherwise law-abiding individuals and their families at risk of falling out of lawful immigration status simply because they cannot organize an international relocation within an extremely short timeframe.

My recommendation

I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

If additional safeguards are necessary to prevent misuse, DHS could consider strengthening eligibility requirements while preserving reasonable flexibility for individuals and families facing unexpected employment termination.

A strong immigration system should protect program integrity while also recognizing the practical realities of people who have spent years building their lives in the United States.

I support efforts to strengthen the U.S. immigration system and promote merit-based immigration. I respectfully believe that retaining a reasonable transition period is consistent with these objectives and allows individuals and families to manage unexpected circumstances with dignity, responsibility, and respect for U.S. immigration laws.

Thank you for considering my comments and the impact of this proposed rule on working professionals and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
​I came to the United States when I turned 22, and I am now 38. For the past 16 years—my entire adult and professional life—I have lived, worked, and paid taxes exclusively in the United States. I do not have earned income anywhere else in the world. My skills, my career, and my life are built entirely around the U.S. economy; if I am forced to return to my birth country now, my family and I will be starting completely from scratch after nearly two decades of contributing here.
​More importantly, I have two children who are U.S. citizens by birth and attend school here. My older child is 6 years old, and he breaks down crying at the mere thought of having to leave the United States someday. My younger child is just 4 months old. They love their country just as deeply as any child whose parents are American—because America is the only home they know.
​For years, families like mine have lived under the weight of an employment-based green card backlog with no end in sight. It is deeply painful that someone who has worked hard for 16 years, followed every rule, and proven beyond doubt that they belong here is forced to wait indefinitely in a multi-decade queue, while others wait less than a year. Yet we have stopped complaining about how unfair that system is. We have accepted the wait, complied with every regulation, and continued contributing to our workplaces and communities.
​However, removing or restricting the 60-day grace period will be devastating for our children and for us, pushing law-abiding families into an impossible trap. Mandatory federal timelines alone take weeks, and even when a skilled professional secures a new job immediately after an unexpected layoff or corporate restructuring, an employer cannot legally file an H-1B transfer overnight. Between corporate background checks, prevailing wage determinations, and mandatory Department of Labor Labor Condition Application (LCA) certification—which takes 7 to 10 business days by statute—the transfer process routinely requires 4 to 8 weeks. Without a 60-day buffer, a routine corporate layoff outside of a worker's control becomes an automatic loss of legal status.
​At the same time, uprooting 16 years of life overnight is logistically impossible. If a family is forced to depart after nearly two decades in this country, wrapping up a household cannot physically or legally happen in a matter of days. Selling a home or ending a lease, closing accounts, pulling a 6-year-old out of elementary school mid-year, and obtaining passports, travel visas, and pediatric medical clearance for a 4-month-old infant takes months. Eliminating the 60-day buffer strips compliant families of the bare minimum time required to either transition employment lawfully or depart safely without accruing unlawful presence. Furthermore, uprooting a family with zero buffer inflicts direct harm and severe psychological, educational, and medical disruption on U.S. citizen children—pulling a first-grader away from his school and peers overnight and interrupting critical early-life pediatric care and immunization schedules for a 4-month-old baby.
​Beyond the toll on immigrant families, forcing abrupt departures directly harms American communities and the broader U.S. economy. Long-term H-1B families who have lived here for 15 or more years are deeply integrated into their local economies—owning homes, signing long-term leases, buying cars, and paying federal, state, Social Security, Medicare, and local property taxes that fund public schools and local infrastructure. Forcing families to abandon their lives overnight leaves landlords with broken leases, triggers distressed home sales or unpaid mortgages and property taxes, pulls consumers out of local businesses, and creates sudden talent vacuums for U.S. employers—all without creating a single job for American workers.
​We are not asking to skip the line or even for an immediate fix to the green card backlog. All we ask is that you show basic grace, humanity, and kindness. Please keep the 60-day grace period intact so that hardworking, law-abiding families, their U.S. citizen children, and the American communities they support are not thrown into sudden, life-altering chaos.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sheetal Kaul
comments.commentText:
Please do not eliminate this grace period.

Introduction

I am an H-1B visa holder and the mother of a two-year-old child. I came here legally 13 years ago, I have worked hard, I pay my taxes, and I have built my career and my family's entire life in the United States. Yet I live every day knowing that a single email from my employer could unravel all of it. The 60-day grace period is the one thin thread of safety my family has. I choose to speak while that thread is getting prepared to be cut.

Background

My comment concerns the proposal to eliminate the up-to-60-day grace period for H-1B workers after a loss of employment. Today, a worker whose job ends before their petition validity expires has up to 60 days to find new employment, change status, or arrange an orderly departure. The proposal would take that window away entirely.

Analysis

What problem does this solve? I sincerely ask the agency to explain what problem eliminating this grace period solves. Sixty days is already painfully short. What it does is turn an involuntary event of losing a job into unlawful presence overnight. People who have done nothing wrong would wake up as rule-breakers through no act of their own.

What it would do to my family. Losing a job is devastating for anyone. On an employment-based visa it is far worse: in the same moment you lose your income, you lose your legal right to be in the place you call home. With AI-driven layoffs sweeping the technology sector, where so many H-1B workers are employed, this is no longer a distant possibility. It is a fear that wakes me up at night. I cannot uproot my child and move my family to another country within hours. Sixty days is already the bare minimum to wind up a life built over many years: to sell a home, cars, and furniture, end leases, buy plane tickets, and somehow prepare a small child for the biggest upheaval of their life. Without it, I would be forced to choose between breaking the law and abandoning everything in a panic. No law-abiding person should be pushed into that kind of desperation.

The pain spreads far beyond the worker. This change hangs over the whole family as a constant, ticking fear. When a child is uprooted overnight, it is not only that child who suffers. Their friends and classmates are left wondering where they went, and other parents are left trying to explain the unexplainable. Older children and young adults feel this loss fully, including U.S. citizens who watch a close friend vanish and are left grieving, confused, and afraid. That is real grief and anxiety for citizens who did nothing to deserve it, and for families who came here legally, in good faith, chasing the opportunity this country promised.

The heaviest harms cannot be counted in dollars. Many of the deepest harms fall on people other than the worker: the dignity and stability of families, and above all U.S.-citizen children torn from their homes, schools, and friends overnight. The burden falls hardest on primary caregivers, who must hold their families together while their own world collapses. I urge the agency to weigh these human harms even where it cannot put a number on them.

What the agency must measure before acting. Before finalizing any change, I ask the agency to estimate and publish: (1) how many H-1B and other affected workers would lose their transition window each year; (2) how many dependent children would be affected, including U.S.-citizen children, who are the future of this country and whose stability the government has a duty to protect; and (3) the mental-health toll on children and caregivers of a sudden, forced relocation with no time to prepare. Losing your job, your income, and your legal status all at once, while trying to shield your children from the fallout, is a crushing psychological burden. If the agency has not estimated these figures, that alone is reason to stop and reconsider. If it has, families like mine deserve to see them.

Recommendation

I respectfully but urgently ask the agency to keep the 60-day grace period and to publish the impact assessment described above.

Conclusion

The 60-day grace period is a deeply humane provision. It is the only thing standing between a family and chaos after a sudden, involuntary loss of job and legal status. Taking it away would throw law-abiding people into desperation and cause immense, lasting anguish for families, for U.S.-citizen children, and for the communities they belong to. I am pleading with the agency: please keep the grace period in place, and look honestly at what taking it away would do to families like mine.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period, because it ignores a basic fact about how an H-1B transfer actually works: even a worker who finds a new job on the very first day after a layoff cannot complete a lawful transfer in zero days.

I know this from experience. After a layoff, finding a willing employer is only the first step. That employer must first obtain a certified Labor Condition Application from the Department of Labor, a process that routinely takes a week or more. Then the employer must prepare and file a new H-1B petition with USCIS, and the worker must wait for a receipt notice before portability protections apply. Background checks, offer letters, and internal approvals add further days. In the fastest realistic case, the paperwork alone takes weeks — and that assumes the worker is hired immediately, which almost never happens. Most people spend the first two or three weeks interviewing, and hiring cycles at many companies run far longer than that.

The current 60 days is already tight. It is barely enough time to interview, receive an offer, and get a petition filed. Zero days is not a stricter standard; it is a calendar impossibility. A worker who does everything right — who is hired on day one by an employer ready to sponsor — would still fall out of status before the required filings could physically be completed. The rule would therefore punish compliance itself, not misconduct, and it would do so regardless of how diligently the worker or the new employer acted.

This is compounded by the government's own timelines. USCIS receipt notices and adjudication do not arrive instantly, and DHS knows it. A rule that demands same-day lawful status while the agency's own processes take days and weeks to acknowledge a filing is internally incoherent. It manufactures status violations out of its own delays.

If DHS is concerned about misuse of the grace period, the proportionate response is to police misuse case by case — the grace period is already discretionary — not to set a deadline that no honest worker can meet. At a minimum, any grace period must be long enough to cover the filing process DHS itself requires. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period.

comments.commentText:
We often speak of borders and policies as if they are merely lines on a map or rules in a book. And strictly speaking, it is true: no nation owes a permanent home to those who arrive from elsewhere. As someone from an OECD country, I understand this logic deeply. I wouldn't expect my own homeland to bend its rules or compromise the livelihoods of its citizens.

But policy on paper looks very different from policy lived out in the flesh. When a person is forced to leave a country they have woven themselves into, they aren't just crossing a line—they are tearing a tapestry apart.

To leave means uprooting a child from the classroom where they were finally starting to belong. It means walking away from friendships that took years to cultivate. It means selling off the car, liquidating the quiet accumulation of a life, and reducing years of effort into numbers on a closing statement.

The quiet tragedies are often the smallest ones. It is the sudden absence at the local mom-and-pop store. It is the missing goodbye to the landscaper, the hairdresser, the caregiver, and the grocery clerk—the familiar faces that make a neighborhood feel like a neighborhood. It is the abrupt end to the charity you gave, the community you served, and the culture you happily assimilated into.

We live in a world that prides itself on order and law. Yet, if a storm rolls in unexpectedly, most of us wouldn't kick a neighborhood cat off our porch. We would let her stay until the rain passed. Surely, the human beings who have poured their hearts, their labor, and their love into our communities deserve at least that same quiet grace while the weather clears.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposal to eliminate the existing grace period for H-1B workers and their dependents.

The proposed change would have consequences far beyond the individual who loses employment. H-1B workers often have spouses and children who have lived in the United States for many years and have built their entire lives here.

• Families need reasonable time to respond to an unexpected job loss. Losing employment is already a serious financial and emotional hardship. Eliminating the grace period could turn an unexpected layoff into an immediate immigration crisis, leaving families insufficient time to find another qualifying employer or make lawful arrangements.

• Children should not bear the consequences of an adult’s unexpected job loss. Many children of H-1B families have spent years, and sometimes their entire lives, attending American schools. Abruptly requiring a family to leave could force children to withdraw from school in the middle of an academic year, disrupting their education, friendships, activities, and sense of stability.

• Many H-1B families have made substantial long-term commitments based on living and working in the United States. They have purchased homes, taken on mortgages, established careers, paid taxes, and built communities. Home ownership does not itself create immigration status, but DHS should recognize the serious practical and financial consequences of requiring such families to leave on extremely short notice.

• A sudden departure could force families into distressed financial decisions. Selling a home, addressing a mortgage, ending leases, transferring children between schools, disposing of personal property, and arranging international relocation cannot realistically be accomplished overnight.

• The impact extends to spouses and children who had no role in the employment termination. A policy affecting one worker can effectively destabilize an entire household, including dependent spouses and minor children.

• Many H-1B workers have been pursuing employment-based permanent residence for years. Families may have invested significant time, money, and effort in the immigration process while continuing to contribute to the U.S. economy. Their reliance and long-term ties should be considered before eliminating an established transition period.

• Employers and workers also need practical time to complete a job transition. A prospective employer may need time for interviews, internal approvals, immigration counsel, and preparation and filing of an H-1B petition. Removing the grace period makes it substantially harder for experienced workers to transition to new employment.

• The existing grace period provides an important safety valve for circumstances outside a worker’s control. It does not guarantee continued employment or permanent residence. It provides limited time for a worker to seek another lawful solution or depart the United States in an orderly manner.

If DHS believes changes are necessary, I respectfully request that it retain a meaningful transition period rather than eliminate it entirely. At minimum, DHS should consider a hardship-based exception for families with minor children, long-term U.S. residence, home ownership, or pending employment-based immigration cases.

Families who have spent years building their lives in the United States should not be forced to dismantle those lives with almost no time to respond to an unexpected job loss. A reasonable grace period promotes lawful compliance while giving families the opportunity to make responsible, orderly decisions.

I respectfully request that DHS consider the significant effects of this proposal on H-1B families, particularly spouses and children who have established their education, homes, careers, and communities in the United States.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shitian Li
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed removal of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and urge DHS to retain it.

I am an international PhD candidate in cancer biology at the University of California, San Diego, conducting research at the Salk Institute. My work on chromatin regulation and cancer immunity has contributed to research published in Cell. I also completed a research internship in the U.S. biotechnology industry in 2026. I comment in my individual capacity, not on behalf of either institution. Although my current F-1 status is not directly affected, H-1B and O-1 status are important future pathways for U.S.-trained scientists.

1. Removing the grace period would damage scientific continuity and workforce mobility.

Biomedical researchers acquire specialized expertise over many years and frequently move among universities, research institutes, hospitals, and biotechnology companies. Changing employers can require securing a new appointment, confirming funding, and preparing an immigration petition. Laboratory closures, grant losses, and layoffs may end legitimate employment without warning.

The existing grace period gives affected workers limited time to seek a new position or other lawful status. It does not itself authorize work. Eliminating it could turn an involuntary employment transition into a status violation the next day. Research programs could lose experienced scientists halfway through a project even when another U.S. employer is willing to hire them. Losses to experiments, collaborations, and research continuity cannot be captured by lost wages alone.

2. The proposal does not adequately justify reversing the 2016 policy.

Section IV.A acknowledges that DHS originally adopted this provision to support high-skilled job mobility and allow American employers to recruit workers without unnecessary departure and readmission. These needs remain. The grace period is limited and discretionary, not permission for indefinite unemployment. DHS should identify evidence that this safeguard itself has materially impaired compliance, rather than treating the existence of a short transition window as a program-integrity problem.

3. DHS's cost-benefit analysis overlooks major consequences.

Section IV.C cites over 1.9 million filings from FY 2018 through May 2026 potentially requiring a grace-period assessment. This is a screening population, not a measurement of adjudicator time actually spent. DHS does not quantify the resulting administrative savings or weigh them against costs of international travel, renewed visa processing, disrupted research, recruiting replacements, and additional immigration proceedings.

Table 3 reports an annual average of 3,795 beneficiaries with new employer petitions filed within 60 days after a previous employer withdrew an approved petition. These reflect concrete efforts to continue lawful employment. Section V.A assumes employers can often hire equally qualified U.S. workers or file new petitions. In specialized biomedical research, replacing someone with years of experience in a particular experimental system or dataset may take months. This assumption needs evidence and sector-specific analysis.

4. The proposal inadequately addresses families and reliance interests.

Section IV.D acknowledges that workers and families made career, housing, and community decisions in reliance on existing rules. Labeling the protection "discretionary" does not eliminate those real-world interests. DHS also acknowledges that it cannot reliably estimate the number of dependents affected. A spouse may be authorized to work for a separate U.S. employer: sudden loss of the principal worker's status can disrupt a second employer and household income. Children, leases, and ongoing obligations cannot be relocated overnight.

5. Less disruptive alternatives would address DHS's stated concerns.

As section IV.C explains, USCIS already may shorten or eliminate a grace period based on individualized circumstances, including fraud, unauthorized work, or national-security concerns. It could also standardize documentation of employment termination, improve reporting, or focus scrutiny on cases presenting compliance risks. Such measures address administrative complexity without requiring otherwise compliant researchers and families to leave immediately after job loss.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal, preserve the existing 60-day discretionary grace period, and undertake a fuller assessment of its effects on universities, research institutes, biotechnology companies, and dependents. The United States benefits when scientists it has trained can transition between legitimate positions without avoidable disruption.

comments.commentText:
Re: Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for Certain Nonimmigrant Workers

I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the current up-to-60-day grace period for certain nonimmigrant workers who lose their employment.

I am commenting as someone who has built a career and a life in the United States over many years. I have made significant long-term commitments here, including a home with a mortgage and a car loan. I also have a child who is a U.S. citizen. My family lives here, spends here, pays taxes here, and contributes to the local and U.S. economy.

My concern is what would happen if an otherwise qualified worker lost a job unexpectedly through a layoff or restructuring.

A job loss does not necessarily mean that the worker is no longer qualified or that their skills are no longer needed. In many industries, layoffs can happen because of budget reductions, reorganizations, mergers, or changes in business priorities. Finding another position is one challenge; completing the immigration process required for the new employment is another. These things cannot always be completed within a few days.

The existing 60-day grace period provides a reasonable transition period for exactly this situation. It gives a worker a limited amount of time to find another qualifying job and gives a prospective employer time to complete the necessary immigration process. Without that period, an unexpected layoff could result in the worker having to leave the United States before a legitimate employment transition can be completed.

That would have consequences beyond the worker. In my own situation, an abrupt departure would not simply mean leaving a job. It could mean dealing with a mortgage, other financial obligations, and the disruption of an established family life. More importantly, my child is a U.S. citizen and has a home, school, community, and family life here. A parent’s involuntary job loss should not, by itself, force an American family to choose between separation and relocating the household.

There is also a practical consequence for U.S. employers. An employer may be willing to hire an experienced worker who has lost a previous job, but the employer needs reasonable time to complete the required immigration process. Eliminating the grace period could cause employers to lose qualified candidates who otherwise could have continued working and contributing in the United States.

I understand DHS’s concern about the administrative burden associated with the current grace period. However, I do not believe eliminating the entire grace period is necessary to address that concern. If the issue is administrative complexity, DHS could consider clearer eligibility requirements, standardized documentation, or simpler procedures for determining and applying the grace period.

The existing provision is also limited. It does not give a worker an unlimited period to remain in the United States without employment. It provides a short window to make a lawful transition after an unexpected employment termination.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to retain the current 60-day grace period. If DHS believes changes are necessary, I encourage the Department to consider narrower administrative reforms that address the identified burden without eliminating the transition period altogether.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing family stability and job transition challenges.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mohamed Noohu
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. I respectfully urge DHS to retain this essential protection and consider its serious consequences for individuals, families, and the American economy.

I have lived and worked in the United States on an H-1B visa for more than 12 years. During this time, I have built my career, paid taxes, contributed to the economy, purchased a home, taken on a mortgage, and established a life with my family. Like many long-term H-1B workers, we have made significant personal and financial commitments based on the immigration rules that have existed for years.

Eliminating the grace period would create enormous uncertainty and hardship.

1. Employment and immigration uncertainty: Losing a job is already difficult. Finding another employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer requires interviews, negotiations, background checks, legal documentation, employer approvals, and USCIS processing. These steps take time. Without the grace period, workers may lose lawful status before having a realistic opportunity to secure new employment.

2. Impact on families and children: H-1B workers have spouses and children who depend on their immigration status. Children attend schools, build friendships, and establish roots in their communities. Sudden departure could disrupt their education, emotional well-being, and future. Spouses may also lose employment opportunities and household income. One person's involuntary job loss should not put an entire family's future at risk.

3. Mortgage and financial hardship: Many long-term H-1B workers own homes, have mortgages, car loans, and other financial obligations. These responsibilities do not disappear when employment ends. Families could be forced to sell homes under pressure, suffer substantial financial losses, default on loans, damage their credit, and lose years of savings and investments. Relocating internationally on short notice would make these challenges even harder.

4. Disregarding years of contribution: People who have spent 10, 12, or 15 years in America have invested their professional and personal lives here. We contribute through taxes, skilled employment, consumer spending, homeownership, and community participation. It is unfair to leave long-term contributors with virtually no transition time after an involuntary job loss.

5. Risk of employer exploitation: Without a grace period, workers could feel forced to accept lower salaries, unfavorable working conditions, or unsuitable jobs simply to maintain immigration status. This would weaken workers' bargaining power and increase their vulnerability to exploitation.

6. Negative impact on the American economy: H-1B professionals contribute to technology, healthcare, engineering, research, and many other industries. Forcing experienced professionals to leave abruptly would result in lost expertise, institutional knowledge, productivity, and talent. It could also discourage skilled workers from investing in long-term careers, homes, and businesses in America.

7. Lack of time for alternative immigration options: Workers need reasonable time to find a new H-1B sponsor, transfer employment, explore a change of status, or pursue other lawful options where eligible. These processes require legal assistance, documentation, employer cooperation, and government processing.

I respectfully request DHS to:

Retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.
Provide reasonable transition protections for workers experiencing involuntary job loss.
Consider additional safeguards for long-term workers with families, mortgages, and substantial financial commitments.
Allow sufficient time to secure new employment or pursue other lawful immigration options.
Evaluate the impact on families, children, homeowners, employers, and the economy before implementing this change.
Conclusion

The United States has been my home for more than 12 years. I have worked hard, paid taxes, contributed to the economy, built a family, purchased a home, and planned my future here in good faith.

Losing a job should not mean potentially losing one's home, disrupting children's education, destabilizing an entire family, and abandoning a life built over more than a decade.

The 60-day grace period is not an unreasonable privilege. It is a necessary safety net that gives workers and families a limited opportunity to navigate an unexpected employment disruption responsibly.

I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period. Please consider the real people, families, children, and communities whose lives could be profoundly affected by this change.

Thank you for your consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the elimination of the 60-day grace period, citing severe hardships for families and the economy.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders. Rather than eliminating this essential protection, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) should extend it to 180 days. The current 60-day period is already inadequate given the realities of today's labor market, and eliminating it would impose disproportionate consequences on legally employed, highly skilled professionals who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.

A temporary job loss should not jeopardize years of lawful employment, professional contributions, and family stability in the United States. H-1B workers follow established immigration rules, pay taxes, support American businesses, and contribute specialized expertise to the U.S. economy. Many have spent years building their careers and communities here while navigating an already complex and restrictive immigration system. Eliminating the grace period would introduce additional uncertainty without meaningfully addressing the underlying challenges of employment-based immigration.

The proposal also fails to account for how professional hiring actually works. Recruiting for specialized positions frequently involves multiple interview rounds, internal approvals, background checks, and immigration sponsorship decisions. These processes can take several months, even for exceptionally qualified candidates. Unlike U.S. workers, H-1B professionals must also secure an employer willing and able to complete the required immigration process. A 60-day deadline is already disconnected from these realities. Eliminating that window entirely would make an involuntary layoff potentially career-ending in the United States, regardless of an individual's qualifications, contributions, or prospects for reemployment.

To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364

I am an H-1B holder, and I strongly oppose eliminating the up-to-60-day grace period after employment ends. I support accurate records, clear immigration rules, and efficient processing. Removing a vital transition period is a disproportionate response to administrative difficulties.

DHS argues that status should remain tied to qualifying employment. A limited opportunity to find another qualifying employer, pursue an eligible immigration option, or arrange an orderly departure is compatible with that purpose. It does not need to authorize unrestricted employment or an indefinite stay.

I can work responsibly, follow immigration rules, and prepare carefully, yet still lose my job because of restructuring or budget cuts. Skilled hiring takes time: rigorous preparation, multiple interviews, scheduling, approvals, background checks, and immigration filings. Even a qualified candidate cannot make an employer finish immediately. Removing the grace period makes the timing of a layoff more important than qualifications or willingness to comply.

H-1B workers also contribute economically. IRS guidance confirms that H-1B wages are generally subject to federal income tax and Social Security and Medicare taxes. As an illustration, $150,000 in wages fully subject to ordinary payroll taxes generates $11,475 in employee Social Security and Medicare taxes and another $11,475 from the employer, before income taxes. This is an example, not my personal tax figure. Actual liability varies. DHS should assess the potential loss of tax revenue when qualified workers must leave instead of moving to another lawful job.

DOL requires H-1B employers to pay at least the higher of the applicable prevailing wage or the employer’s actual wage for similarly qualified and experienced workers. This does not guarantee identical salaries, but it establishes a wage standard. Enforce wage protections and preserve workers’ ability to seek another employer rather than increasing dependence on one employer.

Families cannot unwind their lives on the day a job ends. They have leases, childcare, medical treatment, and children in school. Workers and spouses may be pursuing degrees with tuition already paid. Abrupt departure can interrupt education, disrupt children’s support networks, trigger lease penalties, and require costly last-minute travel. Years invested in education and professional development do not disappear with a layoff, but the opportunity to use those skills here may.

I disagree with Section V.F’s conclusion that family impacts would be negligible. Compare the same family facing job loss with and without a transition period. Lost income is one harm; removing time to stabilize the household or arrange departure creates additional harm attributable to this policy.

Instead of elimination, USCIS should:

1. Standardize separation records: use a short record identifying the worker, employer, petition number, effective employment cessation date, and employer contact. Give the worker a copy and integrate it with existing reporting where possible.
2. Clarify the controlling date: distinguish the last day actively worked, effective termination, paid notice or leave, and later severance or vacation payouts. Officers should not have to infer employment dates from payment dates.
3. Add structured application fields: include a grace-period checkbox, claimed employment end date, and evidence checklist so officers can identify relevant cases immediately.
4. Validate routine information electronically: check missing fields and dates, while focusing additional review on inconsistencies or suspected fraud. Keep human review available for corrections and unusual cases.
5. Protect workers from employer noncooperation: accept alternative evidence, including termination correspondence and payroll records, with a signed declaration where appropriate. Provide an opportunity to correct discrepancies.
6. Pilot and measure improvements: compare processing time, errors, requests for evidence, and costs before removing the protection. Include costs shifted to families, employers, and other government processes.

Section IV.E rejects a documentation alternative partly because verification would remain necessary. The question should be whether verification can become clear and efficient, not whether every administrative task can disappear.

I respectfully request withdrawal of this proposal and preservation of at least the existing up-to-60-day grace period. Improve the documentation process instead of imposing severe consequences on workers and families. Administrative convenience should not outweigh a reasonable opportunity to comply with the law and manage an unexpected job loss.

Statement of Opposition:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers (including H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, and E visa holders). This proposal undermines the economic resilience and competitive advantage of the United States.
1. High-Skilled Talent is a Strategic Asset:
Visas such as the H-1B are specifically allocated to high-skilled workers who drive innovation, research, and economic growth. Companies facing budgetary constraints may make difficult decisions to eliminate high-salaried positions. Forcing highly skilled individuals to depart the country immediately under these circumstances is a severe overreaction that penalizes both the worker and the broader innovation ecosystem.
3. Economic and Administrative Harm to U.S. Employers:
The loss of a 60-day grace period forces skilled workers to step back to their home countries immediately upon job loss. Eliminating it discourages global talent from viewing the U.S. as a stable career destination. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers, because the proposal would not merely shorten a job search. It would destroy the only vetting window a laid-off worker has, and in doing so it would create exactly the fraud and exploitation the H-1B program is supposed to prevent.

Sixty days is not idle time. It is due-diligence time. A worker who has just been laid off must verify that a prospective sponsor is real: that the job exists, that the Labor Condition Application reflects the actual worksite and wage, that the employer has a genuine need and a record of lawful filings, and that the terms offered comply with the law. That checking takes weeks even for an experienced worker with counsel. Sixty days is already tight. Zero days makes it impossible.

Desperation is the fraudster's business model, and this proposal would hand fraudsters their ideal customer. USCIS has long warned about H-1B fraud: shell sponsors filing petitions for jobs that do not exist, intermediaries that "bench" workers without pay, and sponsors that illegally charge workers fees for their own petitions. A worker who must accept the first sponsor promising an immediate filing — or lose lawful status that same day — cannot walk away from a suspicious offer, cannot wait for a second opinion, and cannot check whether the sponsor has been sanctioned before. The rational choice under a zero-day rule is the very choice the law should discourage: sign first, ask questions later.

The harm then compounds. A worker trapped by a sham sponsor may pay unlawful fees, accept below-market wages, or work in a job that does not match the petition. When the petition is denied or revoked, the worker loses status anyway, now burdened with debt and a damaged immigration record. Fear of contact with authorities makes such workers less likely to report the fraud, so the scheme survives to recruit the next laid-off worker. Legitimate employers are harmed too: they must compete against sham sponsors filing low-wage petitions, and USCIS adjudicators must spend scarce resources sorting suspect transfers from legitimate ones, delaying lawful petitions across the board.

Retaining the grace period costs the agency nothing and protects the integrity of the program. It lets a worker reject an exploitative offer without forfeiting lawful status, and it keeps enforcement focused where it belongs: on fraudulent petitioners, not on workers the rule itself pushed toward them. If DHS is concerned about abuse of the grace period, it should target fraudulent sponsors directly. Eliminating the window does the opposite — it manufactures the desperation on which fraud depends.

For that reason, DHS should withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period, and I write from a position the proposal seems to have overlooked entirely: I am an L-1 worker.

I did not come to the United States chasing a job offer. My employer transferred me here — its own decision, for its own business reasons — after years with the company abroad. My family moved across an ocean because the company asked us to. I learned the company's systems, trained its American hires, and built the institutional knowledge that made the transfer worthwhile.

Here is what makes the proposal uniquely devastating for L-1 workers: unlike H-1B workers, we have no portability at all. An H-1B worker who is laid off can at least, in theory, find a new sponsor and transfer. An L-1 worker cannot transfer to a different employer, period. Our status exists only through the single company that petitioned for us. The 60-day grace period is not a convenience for us — it is the only window in which any lawful outcome is possible: time to be sponsored under a new status, to arrange an orderly departure, or to wind down a life the employer itself asked us to build here.

Eliminate that window and the result is immediate unlawful presence on the day of a restructuring decision we did not make, for workers who cannot cure it by finding another job. There is no job search that saves an L-1 worker, because no new employer can hire us in L-1 status. The proposal thus punishes most harshly the workers with the fewest options and the least control — people whose presence here was the employer's initiative in the first place.

This also harms the American companies the proposal claims to protect. Employers use L-1 transfers to bring specialized knowledge into U.S. operations, and they invest heavily in relocating those employees. A zero-day rule makes every transfer a gamble that a single reorganization ends in instant unlawful presence for a trusted employee and the loss of knowledge no replacement hire can quickly supply. Companies will simply stop transferring people here and keep the expertise — and the jobs built around it — abroad.

If DHS is concerned about misuse of the grace period, it already has the tool to address it: the grace period is discretionary, and the agency can deny it case by case where the record supports denial. A blanket zero-day rule does not target abuse. It targets the workers with no alternative, and it should be withdrawn.

Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22

I oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period and ask DHS to withdraw this proposal.

The proposal is presented as a simplification, but in practice it will create more work for the government, not less. Today, a worker who loses a job can often file a change-of-employer or change-of-status petition from within the United States, where USCIS can adjudicate it on the existing record. Employers would also face longer vacancies and repeated filing costs, and workers would bear travel expenses and separation from their homes for a process that serves no security purpose.

A system that pushes lawful, vetted workers out of the country only to process them back in is inefficient by its own terms. The grace period avoids that waste by allowing a timely domestic filing. DHS should withdraw the proposal rather than replace a workable process with a more burdensome one.

I oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period and ask DHS to withdraw this proposal.

Ending a worker's status the day after employment ends leaves no margin for ordinary human error or delay, and the penalty for a mistake can be severe. A worker may learn of a termination late, face a payroll or human-resources processing lag, fall ill, or be unable to travel immediately. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposal to repeal 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and request that DHS retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days for the following reasons:
1. A short grace period is compatible with employment-based status.

In Sections IV.A–B, DHS argues that employment-based classifications are tied to qualifying work and that any period following job loss is inconsistent with their statutory purpose. That does not establish that DHS cannot allow a brief transition between jobs. INA section 214(a) authorizes DHS to regulate the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. The existing provision lasts at most 60 days or the remaining authorized validity period, whichever is shorter; permits only one grace period per authorized validity period; and allows DHS to shorten or eliminate it. The principal worker is generally not authorized to work during this period.

This is not an indefinite right to remain or permission to work without sponsorship. It is a limited opportunity to arrange a lawful transition. DHS should explain why the existing limits and safeguards are insufficient.

2. Administrative savings are not adequately quantified.

Section IV.C cites over 1.9 million petitions and applications from fiscal year 2018 through May 20, 2026, for which the grace period could potentially have applied. Potential applicability does not mean that each case required substantial discretionary review. DHS does not quantify adjudicator hours spent, the frequency of contested determinations, or anticipated savings.

DHS separately estimates about 3,795 workers annually with new Form I-129 petitions filed during a possible grace period, based on a proxy that DHS acknowledges has data limitations. It should distinguish screening from substantive adjudication and compare actual savings with possible additional consular processing, reentry procedures, and immigration proceedings.

3. Immediate loss of status could disrupt U.S. research.

Research appointments may end unexpectedly because of grant changes, institutional reorganizations, or funding decisions. Even when a scientist quickly finds a new job, a prospective employer needs time to complete recruitment, obtain approvals, and prepare an immigration filing. The grace period allows a limited window for those administrative steps.

Without it, a researcher could face immediate departure despite an imminent qualifying offer, interrupting experiments, collaboration, and the transfer of specialized expertise among U.S. universities and businesses. Departure does not accelerate hiring; it may add consular processing and travel delays.

4. Effects on small employers require closer analysis.

DHS's Table 5 identifies 1,852 small entities among 2,886 employers that filed relevant petitions during a possible grace period (64.17%). The proposal assumes employers can hire equally qualified domestic replacements or recruit workers from abroad. That assumption is uncertain for specialized research positions. DHS should evaluate costs from unfilled vacancies, project interruptions, and additional hiring procedures.

5. Families and established reliance interests matter.

In Section IV.D, DHS acknowledges that workers, employers, and dependents may have planned around the existing policy. Sudden job loss can disrupt a spouse's employment, children's schooling, housing, and medical care. Immediate departure also makes it difficult to resolve leases and travel arrangements. DHS states that it cannot reliably estimate how many dependents use the grace period. These impacts warrant fuller analysis, not summary dismissal.

6. Less disruptive alternatives exist.

DHS could standardize evidence of the last employment date, require a simple filing checklist, and retain discretion to shorten or eliminate grace periods for fraud, unauthorized employment, or other adverse factors. Those approaches address administrative concerns while preserving lawful mobility. DHS should evaluate their costs before choosing repeal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the repeal and requests that DHS retain the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22

I oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period. If DHS will not withdraw the proposal in full, I ask it to retain a meaningful grace period instead of reducing it to zero.

A workable alternative is straightforward. First, retain the 60-day grace period for workers already in the United States, so people who relied on the rule in place since 2017 are not upended mid-career. Second, if DHS believes a shorter period is warranted for future cases, adopt no less than 30 days, with a clear rule that a petition filed within that period preserves status while it is pending. Third, provide a transition window of at least 90 days after any final rule takes effect, so workers and employers can adjust hiring, payroll, and travel plans rather than facing an overnight change.

This alternative protects the interests DHS itself invited comment on. It gives families time to avoid sudden school, housing, and medical disruption; it gives small employers and hospitals a realistic chance to retain staff; and it avoids pushing workers into consular processing abroad when a domestic filing would suffice. It also reduces inadvertent overstay, because workers would have a defined filing window instead of a single day to resolve their status.

Zero days is not a transition policy. It is an abrupt cutoff that creates the very instability, agency burden, and local economic harm this docket should avoid. DHS should withdraw the proposal, or at minimum adopt the alternative above.

Eliminating this grace period would create unnecessary uncertainty and could force highly trained researchers to interrupt their work or leave the country, even when another U.S. institution or employer is willing to hire them.

Policies that make it more difficult for these individuals to transition between positions risk undermining that investment and weakening the country's ability to retain scientific talent.

I strongly urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period, which provides a reasonable balance between maintaining immigration compliance and allowing highly skilled workers to navigate unexpected employment transitions without unnecessarily disrupting American research and innovation.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule. I respectfully ask the Department of Homeland Security to consider keeping the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their families, given its value to workers, employers, and the communities they live in.

The grace period keeps talent in the U.S. economy. H-1B professionals are often employed in fields where U.S. employers report persistent shortages, such as engineering, healthcare, research, and technology. When a job ends through no fault of the worker, the 60-day window gives them a reasonable chance to find another sponsoring employer and keep contributing. Without it, skilled people and the investment employers have made in training them may be lost to other countries, which would not serve American competitiveness.

Its impact reaches well beyond the individual worker. H-1B families buy and rent homes, pay property and income taxes, and support local businesses such as restaurants, childcare providers, grocery stores, and service companies. Many are homeowners with mortgage obligations. A sudden requirement to leave could force distressed home sales, lease breaks, and abrupt drops in local spending. These effects would fall on small businesses and neighborhoods as well as on the families themselves.

It protects families from sudden upheaval. A job loss is already one of the most stressful events a household can face. For H-1B families, it can mean children leaving school in the middle of a year, spouses losing their own work authorization, and the end of long-standing community ties within days. The 60-day period gives families a humane, orderly window to plan, whether that means finding a new role or preparing to depart responsibly.

The timing is especially sensitive. Many companies are currently restructuring, and there is real uncertainty about the direction of the technology sector, including questions about the pace of AI investment. In this environment, layoffs often reflect broad business decisions rather than individual performance. Removing the grace period now would penalize skilled workers for market conditions outside their control, at the moment flexibility matters most.

I have a personal example: My family has experienced this firsthand. I was laid off in 2023 and again in 2025 due to company restructuring. During both periods we continued to meet our mortgage and household obligations in Chicago, IL. The ability to remain in the country while searching for work was critical to our family's stability and to our continued contribution to our community.

If the Department has concerns that the current grace period is being misused, I would respectfully suggest considering targeted alternatives, such as clearer reporting or documentation requirements, instead of eliminating a protection that the vast majority of workers rely on in good faith.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to the Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period

To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). This proposal raises serious humanitarian concerns and would impose unnecessary hardship on law-abiding foreign workers and their families.

1. Eliminating the grace period would create inhumane consequences for workers and their families.

Losing a job is already a stressful and financially destabilizing experience. Requiring affected workers to navigate immediate immigration uncertainty on top of sudden unemployment is unnecessarily harsh.

People cannot simply abandon their lives overnight. They need reasonable time to pack their belongings, terminate leases, arrange housing, settle financial obligations, and coordinate international relocation.

For workers with spouses, children, or pets, these challenges become even greater. Families may need to arrange school transfers, medical care, travel documents, and transportation. International pet relocation can require veterinary examinations, vaccinations, health certificates, airline arrangements, and compliance with destination-country import requirements.

These arrangements cannot always be completed immediately, especially during an unexpected job loss.

A worker losing their job should not mean that an entire family must uproot their lives overnight, potentially leaving behind their belongings or beloved pets. Such an outcome would be unnecessarily cruel and disproportionate.

2. The 60-day grace period is a basic humanitarian safeguard, not an unreasonable privilege.

The current grace period provides only a limited opportunity to seek alternative employment, explore lawful immigration options, or prepare for an orderly departure.

Even 60 days may be insufficient for some families to complete an international relocation. Eliminating this limited protection entirely would create additional hardship without adequately accounting for real-world logistical constraints.

3. The proposal would harm American businesses and labor mobility.

Recruitment, technical interviews, background checks, and immigration processing frequently take several weeks or longer. Eliminating the grace period would make it harder for American employers to recruit qualified workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs.

It would also increase employees' dependence on their sponsoring employers, potentially discouraging workers from reporting workplace violations or leaving exploitative employment situations.

4. Immigration enforcement should remain proportionate and humane.

Maintaining immigration compliance is a legitimate government objective. However, enforcement measures should account for the practical realities of employment transitions and the human consequences of abrupt displacement.

There is a fundamental difference between enforcing immigration requirements and imposing immediate hardship on individuals who have complied with the law but unexpectedly lost their jobs.

The government should not create circumstances in which lawful workers face the prospect of abruptly separating from family members, abandoning pets, or leaving behind essential personal belongings simply because their employment ended.

5. DHS should retain the existing 60-day grace period.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

At a minimum, any revised policy should provide sufficient time for affected individuals and families to explore lawful alternatives and arrange a safe, orderly departure when necessary.

The 60-day grace period is not merely an administrative convenience. It is a reasonable protection that recognizes the basic dignity of workers and the practical realities of human life.

Losing a job should not mean losing the ability to leave a country with dignity, keep a family together, or safely bring beloved pets home.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dinesh CHegoni
comments.commentText:
Subject: Personal Impact Statement – Opposition to Eliminating the 60-Day Grace Period

Docket Number: USCIS-2026-0364

To the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period. As someone who cares deeply about my family’s safety, stability, and future, I am extremely concerned about the hardship this change could create for families like mine.

My family has worked hard to build a stable and secure life in the United States. We have responsibilities, financial obligations, and hopes for our future. The possibility of losing employment is already frightening, but removing the 60-day grace period would make an already difficult situation even more devastating.

A job loss should not mean that an entire family’s life must suddenly be turned upside down. Losing employment is not always within a person’s control. Companies downsize, businesses close, and employees can be laid off unexpectedly despite being hardworking and responsible.

The current 60-day grace period provides families with a small but critical opportunity to recover from an unexpected job loss, seek new employment, explore lawful immigration options, and make responsible decisions about their future.

Without that protection, my family could face overwhelming financial hardship, uncertainty about our ability to remain together, and the possibility of losing the stability we have worked so hard to achieve.

The emotional impact would be just as serious. Families should not have to live with the constant fear that one unexpected event could threaten their home, financial security, and future. Parents deserve the opportunity to provide a safe and stable environment for their children without the added fear that a sudden job loss could disrupt everything.

Sixty days is already a very short amount of time to find another employer, complete necessary immigration paperwork, and make life-changing decisions. Eliminating that time entirely would create unnecessary suffering for families who are simply trying to follow the law, work honestly, and contribute to their communities.

I understand the importance of immigration regulations, but I strongly believe those regulations should also recognize the real human consequences of the decisions being made.

We are not just immigration cases or numbers on paperwork. We are families, parents, spouses, and individuals with responsibilities, dreams, and loved ones who depend on us.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period.

Please consider the emotional distress, financial instability, disruption to children’s lives, and potential family separation that eliminating this protection could cause.

Families deserve compassion, stability, and a reasonable opportunity to navigate unexpected hardships without facing immediate consequences that could permanently change their lives.

Thank you for considering my concerns and the impact this proposed change could have on my family and countless others.

Sincerely,

Dinesh Chegoni

I am currently experiencing how important this grace period is. I recently lost my job unexpectedly after working lawfully in the United States for several years. A typical hiring process may involve multiple interviews, internal approvals, background checks, and compensation discussions. After receiving an offer, the new employer still needs time to work with immigration counsel, prepare the Labor Condition Application, wait for certification, and file the H-1B change-of-employer petition.

Without a grace period, an H-1B worker could do everything correctly and still be forced to leave the United States simply because a company's hiring or immigration process cannot be completed immediately.

This would create tremendous uncertainty for workers and their families. It would also hurt U.S. employers because qualified candidates could become unavailable during normal recruiting and immigration processing timelines.

The 60-day grace period is not an indefinite benefit. It is a short and reasonable transition period that allows a worker to find new employment, pursue another lawful immigration option, or prepare to leave the United States in an orderly manner.

For workers like me, the grace period can be the difference between having a realistic opportunity to continue a lawful career in the United States and being forced to leave because of circumstances outside our control.

I respectfully ask DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. If DHS decides to make changes, I strongly urge the agency to preserve a meaningful transition period and protect workers whose employment ended before any new rule becomes effective.

People who have followed the law, maintained valid status, worked, paid taxes, and contributed to the U.S. economy should not lose their ability to remain lawfully in the country overnight because of an unexpected termination.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for certain employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

The existing grace period serves an important practical function in the U.S. immigration and labor system. It allows workers who unexpectedly lose employment a limited amount of time to transition to another employer, change to another lawful status, or depart the United States in an orderly manner.

Eliminating this period would not simply affect individual workers. It would also make it harder for U.S. employers to hire experienced workers who are already present in the United States and already familiar with the U.S. workplace. Professional hiring processes often require several interview rounds, internal approvals, immigration review, and preparation of a new petition. These steps cannot realistically be completed immediately after a termination.

The proposal may also create unnecessary administrative burdens. Without a meaningful transition period, more workers may be forced to file emergency changes of status, leave the United States, or pursue consular processing only because a normal hiring process could not be completed quickly enough. This would create additional work for USCIS, the Department of State, employers, and workers without improving compliance.

Concerns about employer noncompliance, benching, wage violations, or misuse of the H-1B program should be addressed through targeted enforcement against employers that violate existing law. Workers who lose employment because of layoffs, reorganizations, or other business decisions should not lose a reasonable transition period because unrelated employers may have violated program requirements.

The current rule is already limited: it provides a maximum of 60 days and is discretionary. If DHS believes changes are necessary, narrower alternatives—such as additional documentation requirements or reasonable limits on repeated use—would address those concerns without eliminating the protection entirely.

I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing up-to-60-day grace period, or at minimum preserve a meaningful transition period that allows affected workers to pursue new employment, change status, or depart the United States in an orderly manner.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period harms workers, employers, and creates administrative burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364; RIN 1615-AD22), and I urge DHS to withdraw it.

The discretionary 60-day grace period, in place since 2017, serves a narrow and humane purpose. It does not authorize any employment. It simply gives a high-skilled worker whose job ends — most often through a layoff they did not choose — a short window to find a new employer willing to file a petition, apply for a change of status, or make an orderly departure from the United States.

Eliminating it would mean a worker who has lived here lawfully for years, paid taxes, and complied with every rule falls out of status the day after a layoff. In practice, no one can arrange a new petition, move a household, take children out of school, or book an international departure overnight. The predictable results are not better compliance but chaos: families uprooted within days, leases and mortgages broken, and talented workers lost permanently to competing countries that actively recruit them.

It would also make workers more vulnerable to exploitation. If losing a job means losing status the next day, an employer's threat of termination becomes a threat of immediate expulsion, which discourages workers from reporting abuse or unsafe conditions.

Finally, workers and employers have made major life and business decisions in reliance on the framework DHS adopted in 2017. Rescinding it without evidence that the grace period has been abused would punish precisely the people who followed the rules, while adding urgent, avoidable filings to USCIS's own workload.

Please retain the 60-day grace period and withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period causes chaos, harms families, and increases worker vulnerability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nagendra CVenu
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period currently available to certain employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders following the cessation of employment. The proposed rule restores the longstanding principle that temporary employment-based immigration status should remain directly tied to the employment relationship that served as the basis for admission or authorized stay in the United States.

The current grace period creates an exception that allows individuals to remain in the United States for up to 60 days after the employment that justified their nonimmigrant status has ended. While originally intended to provide flexibility, the policy has blurred the connection between visa status and the underlying employment authorization. By eliminating this grace period, DHS is reaffirming that employment-based visas are granted for a specific purpose and should remain contingent upon the continuation of that qualifying employment.

The proposed rule also promotes consistency and integrity within the immigration system. Immigration benefits should be administered according to clear standards that are readily understood by employers, employees, and government agencies alike. A direct link between employment and lawful status reduces ambiguity, discourages misuse of temporary visa categories, and strengthens public confidence in the administration of immigration laws.

Furthermore, DHS has reasonably concluded that eliminating the grace period would reduce administrative burdens associated with adjudicating discretionary requests and determining eligibility for post-employment status retention. Simplifying enforcement and adjudication responsibilities allows agency resources to be directed more efficiently toward core immigration functions, improving program integrity and operational effectiveness.

The United States has a legitimate interest in ensuring that temporary worker programs operate as Congress intended. Individuals who lose qualifying employment retain the ability to seek appropriate immigration benefits before employment ends, depart the United States, or pursue alternative lawful avenues consistent with existing immigration laws. The government is under no obligation to provide an extended period of authorized stay after the fundamental basis for the visa classification no longer exists.

For these reasons, I support DHS's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period and encourage the Department to finalize the rule. The proposal strengthens the integrity of the immigration system, restores a clear connection between immigration status and qualifying employment, promotes administrative efficiency, and advances the consistent enforcement of U.S. immigration law.

comments.commentText:
This comment is submitted anonymously. I oppose the elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers on a ground the proposal never considers: the grace period is what makes an orderly, secure offboarding possible, and removing it increases the risk that American employers' trade secrets and proprietary knowledge leave with the worker.

H-1B workers are, by definition, in specialty occupations. In practice that means they often hold deep, firm-specific knowledge: proprietary codebases, internal systems architecture, client configurations, pricing models, and unreleased product plans. When such an employment ends, a responsible offboarding takes time. Access credentials must be revoked methodically across systems. Company devices and documents must be collected. Ongoing projects must be documented and handed over. Exit procedures under the Defend Trade Secrets Act and company confidentiality agreements must be completed while the worker is still present and reachable.

The 60-day grace period is the window in which all of that happens. It gives the employer time to secure its systems and gives the worker time to cooperate — to return materials, complete handover, and depart in compliance with the law. Eliminate the grace period and that window collapses to zero. A worker who loses their job must leave the country immediately, mid-project, with handover undone and access revocation rushed or incomplete. The employer is left to reconstruct what the worker knew, from colleagues who may not know it, while systems the worker touched remain in an uncertain state.

Worse, abrupt departure creates the very leakage the rule's supporters should fear. A worker given no time to find new status and no orderly exit has every incentive to carry what they know to the next opportunity — and for workers in globally competitive fields, that opportunity is often with a foreign competitor. A worker who departs in an orderly process, with time to comply with confidentiality obligations and an interest in preserving professional relationships and references, is far less likely to take proprietary material. Desperation is the enemy of trade-secret protection; the grace period removes desperation from the equation.

The proposal's stated rationale — that the grace period lets workers linger without authorization — ignores that the worker remains in status during those 60 days precisely so the separation can be handled lawfully. Nothing in the rule explains how employers are supposed to protect proprietary information when the employee holding it must vanish overnight, nor does it reckon with the cost to American firms when their own systems knowledge walks out the door unsecured.

DHS should retain the 60-day grace period. It is not a benefit to the departing worker alone; it is a security measure for the American employer, protecting the trade secrets and proprietary knowledge that make American firms competitive.
